sources.name: Measured homes and a school, Germany
sources.what: Electricity use of 5 homes and 1 school in Konstanz, from building meters.
sources.attribution: Open Power System Data. 2020. Data Package Household Data, version 2020-04-15. https://doi.org/10.25832/household_data/2020-04-15
sources.caveats: Small sample. Meter glitches removed by a documented rule; short gaps interpolated.

sources.name: Commercial buildings, California
sources.what: Offices, a shop, a warehouse, a school and a hospital: calibrated building simulations, averaged over thousands of buildings, per 1,000 m² of floor area.
sources.attribution: Data includes information from the ComStock dataset developed by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) with funding from the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE). doi:10.25984/1876417
sources.caveats: Modelled, not metered. Averages are smoother than any single real building.

sources.name: Home EV charging, Norway
sources.what: 35,000 charging sessions of residents in 12 shared garages: plug-in, plug-out, energy.
sources.used_for: EV visits at homes and residential garages
sources.attribution: Sørensen, Å. L. et al. Electric vehicle charging dataset with 35,000 charging sessions from 12 residential locations in Norway. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.12730566
sources.caveats: Car charging power and battery size are the authors' estimates, not measurements.

sources.name: Workplace EV charging, Netherlands
sources.what: Sessions of regular drivers at an office car park in Utrecht with about 300 charge points.
sources.attribution: Winschermann, L. et al. Electric Vehicle Charging Session Data of Large Office Parking Lot. 4TU.ResearchData. https://doi.org/10.4121/80ef3824-3f5d-4e45-8794-3b8791efbd13
sources.caveats: Non-commercial licence: fine for research, not for a commercial product. Car power not recorded. From 2023 part of the car park was already smart-charged.

sources.name: Wholesale electricity prices
sources.what: Day-ahead market prices for Germany, the Netherlands, France and western Denmark.
sources.caveats: Spot price only. Add grid fees and taxes with the price adder (Eurostat suggestion).

sources.name: Retail tariff components by country
sources.what: Average household and business prices split into energy, network costs and taxes, for 15 countries.
sources.used_for: Price adder suggestions and flat retail tariffs
sources.caveats: Annual averages: real contracts differ. Spot + adder approximates a dynamic tariff without the supplier's margin.

sources.name: Solar generation
sources.what: Output per kWp for 5 locations and 2 roof orientations, computed from 15-minute weather.
sources.attribution: Weather data by Open-Meteo.com (CC BY 4.0); pvlib python; Dobos (2014), PVWatts Version 5 Manual, NREL/TP-6A20-62641
sources.caveats: Modelled, not metered. Checked against PVGIS (EU JRC): 6 of 10 profiles fall within normal year-to-year variation; Amsterdam is about 9% higher and Los Angeles about 9% lower (causes unverified). Treat solar yields as accurate to about ±10%.

sources.name: Day-ahead solar forecasts
sources.provider: Open-Meteo Previous Runs API + pvlib (NREL PVWatts method)
sources.what: For each solar profile above: the output predicted from the weather forecast made 24 hours earlier, through the same solar model.
sources.used_for: Realistic forecasts (what a controller would have been told)
sources.attribution: Weather data by Open-Meteo.com (CC BY 4.0); pvlib python; Dobos (2014), PVWatts Version 5 Manual, NREL/TP-6A20-62641
sources.caveats: Forecasts are hourly, repeated over 15-minute steps. Hours missing from the archive are filled with the actual solar 24 h earlier.

sources.name: CityLearn typical year, California
sources.what: 17 home loads, solar per kW, two price series and EV schedules for one typical year.
sources.caveats: Location and year not documented. EV schedules look synthetic. 'Dynamic' price origin unknown.

sources.name: Data center load, Colorado (HPC)
sources.provider: National Laboratory of the Rockies (formerly NREL), ESIF data center
sources.what: IT power and whole-facility power (IT + cooling + pumps + HVAC + lights) of a ~2.5 MW liquid-cooled supercomputer data center.
sources.attribution: Clark, S. and Strelka, J. NLR HPC Facility Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) Data. National Laboratory of the Rockies, 2026. https://data.openei.org/submissions/8616
sources.caveats: One facility. Cooling is best-in-class (PUE about 1.07-1.08, industry average 1.54), so the facility profile understates cooling for a typical site. HPC jobs, not a cloud or AI-inference mix.

sources.name: US large-customer tariff (Xcel Colorado)
sources.provider: OpenEI Utility Rate Database (U.S. DOE / NREL)
sources.what: Xcel Energy Colorado Schedule PG 2024: seasonal energy price and a 14-18 h peak-window demand charge, as 15-minute profiles.
sources.used_for: Data center and large commercial tariffs
sources.caveats: One utility, one year. Weekend peak window and the demand interval taken from URDB as listed (not checked against Xcel's tariff book). Fixed monthly charge not modelled.

sources.name: Heat demand and heat pump efficiency, Europe
sources.what: Hourly heat demand for space heating and hot water (single- and multi-family houses) and the coefficient of performance (COP) of air- and ground-source heat pumps, for Germany, the Netherlands, France and Denmark.
sources.attribution: Ruhnau, O., Hirth, L., Praktiknjo, A. (2019). Time series of heat demand and heat pump efficiency for energy system modeling. Scientific Data 6, 189. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-019-0199-y. Data: Open Power System Data, When2Heat 2023-07-27.
sources.caveats: National synthetic profiles from gas standard load profiles and weather, not a measured house: smoother than any single home. The space / hot-water split and the effective COP for the mix are our computation from the dataset's columns. One missing hour per year is interpolated.

sources.name: Time-variable network fees, Germany (§14a Modul 3)
sources.provider: Netzgesellschaft Düsseldorf; Stadtwerke Mosbach (published price sheets)
sources.what: The three-tier network fee (low / standard / high) German grid operators must offer to homes with a controllable device and a smart meter since April 2025.
sources.used_for: Optional network fee on top of the import price
sources.coverage: 2026 price sheets, applied to every year
sources.attribution: Netzgesellschaft Düsseldorf mbH, Netzentgelte Strom gültig ab 01.01.2026 (18.12.2025); Stadtwerke Mosbach GmbH, Preise für die Nutzung des Stromverteilnetzes, gültig ab 1. Januar 2026 (status October 2025).
sources.caveats: Each grid operator sets its own tiers and windows; these are two examples. Net of VAT. The fixed Modul 1 reduction is not modelled.

excluded.name: CityLearn 15-second datasets
excluded.why: Not real 15-second data: the files' own metadata says they are hourly values split evenly into 15-second slices.

excluded.name: Norwegian day-ahead prices (Energy-Charts, NO1)
excluded.why: Published for private and internal use only; commercial use prohibited. Not open data.

excluded.name: Caltech ACN-Data (GitHub copy)
excluded.why: No licence attached; redistribution terms unclear. The official API needs a personal key.

excluded.name: Google data center power traces
excluded.why: Open (CC BY 4.0) but only reachable through BigQuery with a cloud account. Candidate for later.

rules: No fake resolution: if the time step is finer than the data, values are repeated and the run says so.
Same season, same weekday: sources from different years are aligned on season and weekday; each run lists the real dates used.
European times use CET (UTC+1) without summer time; California data uses Pacific standard time; Colorado data (data center, US tariff) uses Mountain standard time.
Every default parameter cites its source; example sizes in the example sites are marked as choices.

checks.what: Engine vs CityLearn, same home without a battery
checks.result: Grid power within 0.0001 kW and cost within 0.001% over 47 hours (automated test).

checks.what: Eurostat components vs published all-in household price
checks.result: Energy + network + taxes reproduces the total within about 0.5% (DE, NL, FR, DK).
